query: Single-phase ZrB2 benefits from strong Zr–B and B–B interactions and a high melting point, but it requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and does not readily meet application requirements on its own. Earlier studies sought to lower the required temperature, yet the resulting materials remained vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion, while reported preparation temperatures generally remained above 1700 °C. Under the constraints of lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength and structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath, what single intervention could overcome these limitations? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome compared with single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, applicable preparation and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment evaluating final body quality, structural integrity, oxidation, and liquid-metal corrosion that would falsify the hypothesis if its predictions were not observed.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored ultra‐high pressure sintering (UHPS) process combined with a controlled rapid quenching step will produce single‐phase ZrB₂ with a built-in, nanostructured surface ZrO₂ sealing layer that not only allows lower-temperature densification (around 1450 °C versus >2300 °C) but also simultaneously improves mechanical strength, oxidation resistance, and liquid metal (plating) corrosion durability compared with both high‐temperature sintered and traditional sintering‐aided specimens.
generation.material_initial_state: High-purity ZrB₂ powder prepared for densification without sintering aids.
generation.intervention: Apply UHPS at 15 GPa and 1450 °C for a short hold (≈10 min) followed by a rapid controlled quenching process to induce an in situ nanostructured ZrO₂ layer at the surfaces and grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Sintering under ultra‐high pressure at 1450 °C with immediate quenching to ambient temperature; subsequent service conditions include high-temperature oxidation tests (up to ~1100 °C) and exposure to a representative liquid plating bath environment at service temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: Ultra‐fine grain structure with high dislocation density (from plastic deformation during UHPS) and an engineered, continuous nanolayer of ZrO₂ forming at grain boundaries and particle surfaces during quenching.
generation.mechanism: The UHPS process refines grain size and induces high dislocation densities that enhance mechanical properties and raise the oxidation threshold. The rapid quench promotes controlled surface oxidation that forms a coherent and protective ZrO₂ nanolayer, sealing grain boundaries against oxygen ingress and inhibiting wetting and corrosion by the liquid metal plating bath.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with conventional high-temperature sintered ZrB₂ and lower-temperature, sintering-aid modified specimens (e.g., Ni-aided systems), the UHPS-plus-quenching specimen will display similar or improved strength, a threshold oxidation temperature elevated by ~250 °C or more, and significantly reduced degradation when exposed to a liquid plating environment, as evidenced by lower corrosion rates and stable mechanical integrity over extended service durations.
generation.baseline: Traditional single-phase ZrB₂ sintered above 2300 °C and lower-temperature specimens produced with liquid-phase sintering aids (e.g., Ni in ZrB₂–HfC ceramics) that suffer from inferior interfacial bonding and corrosion resistance.
generation.boundary: The process is expected to be effective for preparing dense ZrB₂ ceramics for applications operating up to around 1100 °C (oxidation challenge) and for service in aggressive liquid metal (plating) environments; its durability under cyclic thermal and corrosive conditions over hundreds of hours will define its long-term applicability.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from UHPS studies (PMC8867202) supports enhanced mechanical and oxidation properties via grain refinement and dislocation engineering, and liquid-phase sintered systems (PMC6213270) show the pitfalls of sintering aids on interfacial bonding, the formation and stability of the in situ ZrO₂ nanolayer under rapid quenching and its behavior during prolonged liquid metal exposure remain untested. This study extends the UHPS approach by integrating a rapid quench, a novel element that has not been systematically evaluated in this context.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of specimens: (a) conventional high-temperature sintered ZrB₂ (>2300 °C), (b) lower-temperature ZrB₂ sintered with liquid-phase sintering aid (e.g., Ni-based), and (c) ZrB₂ processed by UHPS at 1450 °C with rapid quenching. Subject all specimens to accelerated aging tests including cyclic high-temperature oxidation (up to ~1100 °C) and immersion in a simulated liquid plating bath (e.g., molten metal at representative service temperatures) for extended durations (e.g., 500 hours).
measurements: Mechanical properties (hardness, fracture toughness) before and after exposure
Oxidation scale thickness and compositional analysis (using SEM/EDS and XRD)
Corrosion depth and mass change during liquid metal exposure
Microstructural analysis (TEM/SEM) to assess the continuity and durability of the ZrO₂ nanolayer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the UHPS-plus-quench specimens do not exhibit a significantly higher oxidation temperature threshold (≥250 °C improvement), maintain equal or superior mechanical properties, and show lower corrosion or mass loss compared to both the high-temperature sintered and sintering-aid specimens under the identical test conditions, then the hypothesis that the rapid quench induces a protective ZrO₂ nanolayer contributing to enhanced performance will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractZrB2–HfC ceramics have been fabricated using the liquid phase sintering technique at a sintering temperature as low as 1750 °C through the addition of Ni. The effects of HfC addition on the microstructure and mechanical properties of ZrB2–based ceramics have been investigated. These ceramics were composed of ZrB2, HfC, Ni, and a small amount of possible (Zr, Hf)B2 solid solution. Small HfC grains were distributed among ZrB2 grain boundaries. These small grains could improve the density of ZrB2–based ceramics and play a pinning role. With HfC content increasing from 10 wt % to 30 wt %, more HfC grains were distributed among ZrB2 grain boundaries, leading to weaker interface bonding among HfC grains; the relative density and Vickers hardness increased, and flexural strength and fracture toughness decreased. The weak interface bonding for 20 and 30 wt % HfC contents was the main cause of the decrease in both flexural strength and fracture toughness.Keywords: ZrB2–HfC ceramics, hot pressing, sintering aid, microstructure, mechanical properties

AbstractZirconium diboride (ZrB2) is considered as one of the most promising ultra‐high temperature materials for the applications in extreme environments. However, the difficulty in fabrication of ZrB2 limits its industrial applications. In this study, fully dense and grain‐refined ZrB2 is prepared under ultra‐high pressure of 15 GPa at low temperature of 1450 °C. The as‐prepared ZrB2 exhibits excellent mechanical and oxidation‐resistant properties. Compared with raw powder, the grain size decreases 56%. Compared with high‐temperature sintered control specimen beyond 2000 °C, the hardness and fracture toughness increase about 46% and 69%, respectively, the dislocation density increase 3 orders of magnitude, while the grain size considerably decrease 96%. According to work hardening, Hall–Petch and Taylor dislocation hardening effects, the refined grains, substructures, and high dislocation density caused by plastic deformation during sintering can enhance the mechanical properties. The unique structure contributes to a threshold oxidation temperature increase of ≈250 °C relative to the high‐temperature sintered ZrB2, achieving one of the highest values (1100 °C) among the reported

In summary, fully‐dense and finer‐grained ultra‐high temperature ZrB2 ceramics were successfully fabricated under ultra‐high pressure at low temperature. The dominant densification mechanism was proposed and proved as the plastic deformation‐induced dislocation multiplication and grain boundary sliding. The proportion of dislocation cells, substructures, and small‐angle grain boundaries gradually increased when the sintering temperature reached the critical temperature of 1450 °C. ZrB2 sintered under 15 GPa at the optimized temperature of 1450 °C holding 10 min showed full density, fine microstructures, high dislocation density, and excellent mechanical properties. The grain size of as‐sintered ZrB2 ceramics decreased ≈56% compared with the raw powder. The microstructure observation after indentation and properties characterization after heat treatment proved that the high dislocation density, finer grain size, and high prestress induced by UHPS contributed the enhancement of mechanical properties.
